handoff.summary: Four additional definitions: physical labor productivity, unit compensation cost, economic profit after opportunity costs, finite-increment marginal cost. Named output measures are independent source definitions; none predicts output, estimates a demand/cost function or asserts equilibrium. Earlier 19 models retained without renamed profiles.

assumptions: Source definition: output compared with labor time used to create it.
Application profile: homogeneous physical output measure with consistent quality. Actual hours worked summed across included people, over matching output interval.

gaps: New labor_hours_worked and physical_output_per_labor_hour meanings and unit/h; produced_quantity reuses b02 definition. Runtime duration cannot silently stand for a labor-time sum without compatible meaning/context.

models.inverse_notes: Q=LP*H given LP>=0,H>0, unique. H=Q/LP for LP>0,Q>0; recovered H>0. Published check LP=3,H=100 recovers Q=300 and forward 3. At Q=LP=0 any H>0 fits; LP=0,Q>0 incompatible; Q=0,LP>0 implies H=0 outside domain. These are accounting port inverses, not a production function that holds Q or productivity fixed after changing labor input.
limitations: Not the marginal product of labor, an individual worker ability measure, or a causal effect of working another hour.
Aggregate heterogeneous output requires a separately defined real-output index or value measure; nominal revenue changes must not be mistaken for physical productivity.
No constant production rate, future output or profit-maximization claim.

references.method: Published teaching result 3 birdhouses/hour retained. Annual total output 300 and actual labor hours 100; source amounts are exact hypothetical values, tolerance floating only.
references.provenance: https://www.bls.gov/k12/productivity-101/content/birdhouses/home.htm, first labor-productivity example and final table year 1.

references.method: Published teaching result 5 birdhouses/hour retained. A different scenario measures changed output with same labor hours; no predictive equation for technical change curated.
references.provenance: https://www.bls.gov/k12/productivity-101/content/birdhouses/home.htm, example with easier cuts and final table year 2.

references.method: Independent task ledger: three workers each complete sixteen identical units during two hours; each completes eight per worked hour. Pooled output 48 and summed hours six retain eight, whereas dividing by two elapsed hours would be wrong.
references.provenance: Curator synthetic production/task ledger; no observed labor productivity data.

rejection_cases.reason: No positive labor input; output per worked hour undefined.

relationship.original_equation: Labor productivity = physical output / labor hours worked (Beth's Birdhouses: 300/100=3).
relationship.translation_notes: Introduced Q,H,LP map source physical output, hours worked and labor productivity. Source generic real-output definition is serialized in homogeneous physical units as explicitly demonstrated by birdhouses, not nominal sales revenue. Dimensions U/T, unit unit/h. Labor hours are summed across people; e.g. three workers each working two hours contribute six labor hours even if elapsed clock time is two hours. Source output-per-hour definition does not require constant hourly productivity during the interval. No input is a device active duration or time-series sample count.

sources.evidence: Labor productivity compares output to labor used; formula description specifies real output divided by hours worked, supported by physical-unit birdhouse example.

models.summary: Output per aggregate labor hour for a homogeneous product/service. A descriptive ratio of measured outputs and labor input; other production inputs may also contribute.
models.title: Labor productivity in homogeneous physical output per hour worked

variables.context: Same production boundary (firm/process or homogeneous-output sector), good/service quality and accounting interval. Q counts homogeneous units produced, H sums actual labor time worked by every included worker on that output. Concurrent workers' hours add; H is not wall-clock elapsed duration, payroll-paid leave or just one worker's schedule.
variables.definition: Homogeneous physical goods/services produced during the interval; quality and output boundary held explicit.
variables.domain: Finite nonnegative; not heterogeneous unweighted products or units merely sold.
variables.source_symbol: Introduced Q = output in source physical example

variables.context: Same production boundary (firm/process or homogeneous-output sector), good/service quality and accounting interval. Q counts homogeneous units produced, H sums actual labor time worked by every included worker on that output. Concurrent workers' hours add; H is not wall-clock elapsed duration, payroll-paid leave or just one worker's schedule.
variables.definition: Total actual work hours of the included labor population used in producing Q over the same interval.
variables.domain: Finite strictly positive; includes all relevant workers within scope, with actual worked-time convention.

variables.context: Same production boundary (firm/process or homogeneous-output sector), good/service quality and accounting interval. Q counts homogeneous units produced, H sums actual labor time worked by every included worker on that output. Concurrent workers' hours add; H is not wall-clock elapsed duration, payroll-paid leave or just one worker's schedule.
variables.definition: Interval output divided by aggregate labor hours worked, in homogeneous physical units per hour.
variables.domain: Finite nonnegative average output per labor hour.

assumptions: Source definition: labor compensation divided by the output it produces; compensation includes the chosen complete wage/benefit scope.
Application profile: homogeneous physical output, nonnegative covered compensation, matching period and worker support.

gaps: New labor_compensation_amount and labor_compensation_per_output_unit meanings; homogeneous physical output context required. Existing average_total_production_cost quantity cannot bind unless cost-scope equality is independently proven.

models.inverse_notes: C_L=ULC*Q for ULC>=0,Q>0; Q=C_L/ULC requires ULC>0,C_L>0 and Q>0. Ledger check ULC=5,Q=180 gives C_L=900; forward 5. At C_L=ULC=0 any positive Q fits; ULC=0,C_L>0 incompatible; C_L=0,ULC>0 implies excluded Q=0. Hourly representation requires actual H>0 matching both C_L and Q, and is a derived consistency identity, not an extra forecasting model.
limitations: Does not estimate wages, benefits or output; does not attribute productivity changes solely to labor.
Official sectoral ULC indices and real-output aggregates require their own output concepts, base periods and normalization. No mapping from total production cost or price alone.

references.method: Independent source-supported alternate route: three people each work ten hours, earn 20 dollars/hour wage plus 10/hour benefits, and each produces six units per worked hour. Complete hourly compensation is 30; physical labor productivity six; ratio is 5 dollars/unit. Separate ledgers give compensation 900 and output 180. Explicit benefits make omission detectable.
references.provenance: Curator synthetic matched compensation and task ledger using BLS equivalent hourly representation.

references.method: Independent source-supported hourly route: sixteen worked hours at 24 dollars/hour wages plus 6/hour benefits, with fifteen units per hour. Compensation/hour 30 divided by output/hour 15 yields 2. Amounts independently accumulate to 480 compensation and 240 units.
references.provenance: Curator synthetic materially different compensation/output profile.

references.method: Ideal algebraic boundary with zero covered paid/imputed compensation and positive physical output; zero labor-compensation expense per unit. This does not imply labor has zero opportunity cost.
references.provenance: Curator admitted nonnegative-compensation boundary, not a claim about BLS imputation for actual self-employed workers.

rejection_cases.reason: No output units over which to define labor compensation per unit.

relationship.locator: Productivity 101: Unit labor cost, compensation prose and formula descriptions
relationship.original_equation: Unit labor cost = labor compensation / output; equivalently compensation per hour / output per hour.
relationship.translation_notes: Introduced C_L,Q,ULC map source compensation, output and unit labor cost. Physical-unit application follows source's description of cost to produce one unit; currency/U dimensions. Numerator is current-dollar labor compensation including covered benefits; denominator is physical production, not selling price or nominal revenue. Equivalent representation (C_L/H)/(Q/H) is a qualified inverse/consistency route only for H>0 with the same labor population. This is not the b02 average-total-cost record: only independently defined compensation is included, even when the monetary units match.

sources.evidence: Unit labor cost divides labor compensation by output; compensation can include wages and benefits. Equivalent hourly-compensation/output-per-hour representation uses identical labor/output supports.

models.summary: Defined labor-compensation amount per homogeneous unit produced. Keeps labor expense distinct from all other production costs and from aggregate ULC indices based on real value-added output.
models.title: Labor compensation cost per physical unit of output

variables.context: Same homogeneous physical output and production interval, labor population and compensation scope; current USD compensation includes all covered wages and employer benefits attributable to producing Q. Output units/quality are fixed; labor compensation is a period flow, not wage rate, total production cost or price-adjusted output value.
variables.definition: Complete covered labor compensation (wages and benefits) attributable to this physical output during the interval.
variables.domain: Finite nonnegative; specify included paid/imputed compensation and avoid omitting benefits while claiming complete compensation.

variables.context: Same homogeneous physical output and production interval, labor population and compensation scope; current USD compensation includes all covered wages and employer benefits attributable to producing Q. Output units/quality are fixed; labor compensation is a period flow, not wage rate, total production cost or price-adjusted output value.
variables.definition: Homogeneous physical output produced during the same compensation interval.
variables.domain: Finite strictly positive with fixed product/service quality.

variables.context: Same homogeneous physical output and production interval, labor population and compensation scope; current USD compensation includes all covered wages and employer benefits attributable to producing Q. Output units/quality are fixed; labor compensation is a period flow, not wage rate, total production cost or price-adjusted output value.
variables.definition: Current-dollar compensation per unit of matching physical production.
variables.domain: Finite nonnegative; not total per-unit cost, unit wage or a dimensionless index.

assumptions: Source definition: account for both explicit and implicit resource costs, distinguishing economic from accounting profit.
Application profile: nonnegative revenue and cost amounts, complete disjoint expense/opportunity categories and consistent monetary/temporal basis.

gaps: New revenue, explicit/implicit opportunity-cost and economic_profit meanings; USD alone insufficient. Do not bind accounting break-even output to zero economic_profit without additional cost-boundary evidence.

models.inverse_notes: R=pi_e+C_exp+C_imp, C_exp=R-C_imp-pi_e, C_imp=R-C_exp-pi_e with recovered inputs nonnegative and original monetary/alternative scope retained. Additive unique solutions; no denominator or root. Published substitution pi_e=-10000,C_exp=85000,C_imp=125000 recovers R=200000, forward -10000. At pi_e=0, R equals both cost categories together; each missing input is uniquely determined if others known. Only profit plus one component cannot identify remaining two. Inversion does not establish the true best alternative or a causal effect of changing revenue.
limitations: Does not value alternatives, establish their feasibility or quantify subjective opportunity costs without external evidence.
Not discounted project value, bank balance change or a recommendation to enter/exit an activity. Reference example's hypothetical expected revenue is used solely as a published arithmetic oracle.

references.method: Published -10000 dollars/year economic profit retained. Source 50000 office+35000 clerk sum to explicit 85000; source accounting profit 115000 is below 125000 forgone salary by 10000. Oracle is the published teaching outcome, not a new forecast.

Independent opportunity ledger: after paying 20000 resource bills, venture gives owner the same 40000 amount as the best alternative use of the owned resources. Neither alternative has an economic surplus over the other, so zero economic profit.
references.provenance: Curator synthetic zero-economic-profit boundary, with alternative valuation supplied for this case only.

references.method: Independent paired alternatives: venture's owner residual 43000 versus 40000 outside opportunity leaves a 3000 advantage. This is a constructed comparison under fixed feasible alternatives, not a prediction.

rejection_cases.reason: Implicit opportunity cost missing; cannot silently claim it is zero.

relationship.locator: Section 7.1 distinction and Work It Out Step 3
relationship.original_equation: Economic profit = total revenues - explicit costs - implicit costs.
relationship.translation_notes: Introduced R,C_exp,C_imp,pi_e map source prose labels. Currency-currency-currency=currency for the same interval and price basis; no per-year numeric multiplier is introduced. Implicit cost is an opportunity-cost amount, not necessarily a cash payment or recorded book expense. Separately named economic profit is not an alternative solve direction of b02 linear break-even: no price-volume/linear-cost assumption is made and an additional opportunity-cost boundary changes the scientific meaning. If C_imp=0, accounting-profit residual is a qualified boundary, not a separate clone.

sources.evidence: Economic profit deducts explicit and implicit opportunity costs from revenue. The legal-practice teaching example gives 200000 revenue, 85000 explicit expense, 125000 foregone salary and -10000 annual economic profit; accounting profit differs.

models.summary: Signed residual after paying explicit expenses and valuing foregone opportunities of owned inputs. Distinct from accounting operating income and cash flow; no recommendation or profitability forecast.
models.title: Economic profit after explicit and implicit costs

variables.context: Same enterprise/activity and accounting interval, current USD or explicitly fixed real-USD price basis, revenue boundary and feasible alternative-use/opportunity-cost valuation date. Explicit and implicit costs are disjoint and complete; implicit costs describe the best forgone use of owned resources, without double counting paid expenses.
variables.definition: Revenue for the activity and interval on the declared recognition/price basis.
variables.domain: Finite nonnegative revenue in this ordinary sales profile.

variables.context: Same enterprise/activity and accounting interval, current USD or explicitly fixed real-USD price basis, revenue boundary and feasible alternative-use/opportunity-cost valuation date. Explicit and implicit costs are disjoint and complete; implicit costs describe the best forgone use of owned resources, without double counting paid expenses.
variables.definition: Complete out-of-pocket resource costs on the source's explicit-cost convention for the activity/interval.
variables.domain: Finite nonnegative; classifications, recognition and scope independently supplied.

variables.context: Same enterprise/activity and accounting interval, current USD or explicitly fixed real-USD price basis, revenue boundary and feasible alternative-use/opportunity-cost valuation date. Explicit and implicit costs are disjoint and complete; implicit costs describe the best forgone use of owned resources, without double counting paid expenses.
variables.definition: Opportunity cost of using owned resources rather than their best feasible forgone uses over the same interval.
variables.domain: Finite nonnegative amount under declared alternative/cost convention; include relevant forgone income/leisure if within scope; not a default parameter.

variables.context: Same enterprise/activity and accounting interval, current USD or explicitly fixed real-USD price basis, revenue boundary and feasible alternative-use/opportunity-cost valuation date. Explicit and implicit costs are disjoint and complete; implicit costs describe the best forgone use of owned resources, without double counting paid expenses.
variables.definition: Signed revenue residual after explicit expenses and all declared implicit opportunity costs.
variables.domain: Finite signed, including negative economic loss or zero profit after opportunity costs.

assumptions: Source definition: finite change in cost divided by finite change in output; a wider increment is an average over additional units.
Application comparison: same short-run cost function, holding technology, fixed inputs, input prices, quality and accounting period length fixed; no demand or equilibrium assumption.

gaps: New finite_increment_marginal_cost meaning; total_production_cost and produced_quantity reused from b02 with distinct endpoint contexts. Scalar context equality alone cannot establish identical cost functions.

models.inverse_notes: C2=C1+MC_d*(Q2-Q1) and C1=C2-MC_d*(Q2-Q1) for known MC_d and Q2>Q1>=0, recovering nonnegative costs. Q2=Q1+(C2-C1)/MC_d requires MC_d!=0 and recovered Q2>Q1; Q1=Q2-(C2-C1)/MC_d also requires MC_d!=0 and 0<=Q1<Q2. Check MC_d=4,C1=320,Q1=40,Q2=60 gives C2=400; forward four. At MC_d=0,C1=C2 any admissible output interval fits, so quantity endpoints are not identified; MC_d=0,C1!=C2 incompatible. No root branches. Original denominator guard persists in every inverse; no derivative or economic behavior is solved.
limitations: Does not infer a continuous marginal-cost derivative or constant individual-unit marginal costs throughout a multi-unit interval.
Two dated observations with changed technologies/input prices do not alone establish this cost-schedule comparison. No profit-maximizing quantity or marginal-revenue equality asserted.

references.method: Published 11.50-dollar marginal cost of second widget retained. Exact teaching values; tolerance floating only.
references.provenance: https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/7-3-costs-in-the-short-run, Average and Marginal Costs prose and Table 7.8.

references.method: Published 4-dollar/haircut result retained for twenty additional haircuts. Independent resource route: one additional barber-day costs 80 and contributes twenty additional haircuts in the source schedule; allocating 80 over twenty units gives four, without claiming each local derivative is four.
Limiting identity: two alternative output levels with the same supplied total cost have zero finite incremental cost; no claim that the whole cost schedule is flat.

rejection_cases.reason: Reversed ordering outside the declared additional-output profile; swapping both endpoint pairs would be a qualified view, not new model.

relationship.locator: Section 7.3, Average and Marginal Costs; explicit 40-to-60 haircut increment
relationship.translation_notes: Introduced C1,C2=TC(Q1),TC(Q2), MC_d=source finite-change MC. Dimensions (currency-currency)/(U-U)=currency/U. Quantities are ordered Q2>Q1 to name an additional-output interval; reversing both endpoints gives same secant but is not separately curated. Nonnegative total-cost levels do not impose a signed-derivative claim; MC_d retains whatever finite cost difference is supplied. Fixed inputs, input prices and quality are held unchanged to compare one cost schedule (ceteris paribus), not inferred from matching labels. Q1=0 is allowed if the actual source cost at zero, including fixed costs, is provided; do not assume it is zero.

sources.evidence: Finite-change marginal cost divides change in total cost by additional units. Widget example reports 11.50 for moving from one to two units; haircut example reports 4 per haircut for 40-to-60 units. This does not specify the derivative within that whole interval.

models.summary: Average additional cost per additional physical unit between two distinct output levels on the same cost schedule. Unit increment gives the cost of that next discrete unit; no continuous derivative or constant marginal cost within a larger interval implied.
models.title: Finite-increment marginal production cost

variables.context: Same short-run production technology/fixed-input regime, input-price vector, product quality, cost convention and accounting interval duration at both output levels. C1,C2 are costs of producing alternative quantities in that same regime; quantities are output levels, not sequential calendar observations on different cost schedules.
variables.definition: Total production cost for the lower output level on the declared cost schedule.
variables.domain: Finite nonnegative with the same complete cost convention as C2.

variables.context: Same short-run production technology/fixed-input regime, input-price vector, product quality, cost convention and accounting interval duration at both output levels. C1,C2 are costs of producing alternative quantities in that same regime; quantities are output levels, not sequential calendar observations on different cost schedules.
variables.definition: Total production cost for the higher output level on the same cost schedule.
variables.domain: Finite nonnegative; source doesn't supply a universal slope sign guard.

variables.context: Same short-run production technology/fixed-input regime, input-price vector, product quality, cost convention and accounting interval duration at both output levels. C1,C2 are costs of producing alternative quantities in that same regime; quantities are output levels, not sequential calendar observations on different cost schedules.
variables.definition: Lower homogeneous output level for the same production interval length/regime.
variables.domain: Finite nonnegative; zero permits a genuine no-output level with possible fixed cost.

variables.context: Same short-run production technology/fixed-input regime, input-price vector, product quality, cost convention and accounting interval duration at both output levels. C1,C2 are costs of producing alternative quantities in that same regime; quantities are output levels, not sequential calendar observations on different cost schedules.
variables.definition: Higher homogeneous output level on the same cost schedule.

variables.context: Same short-run production technology/fixed-input regime, input-price vector, product quality, cost convention and accounting interval duration at both output levels. C1,C2 are costs of producing alternative quantities in that same regime; quantities are output levels, not sequential calendar observations on different cost schedules.
variables.definition: Signed average change in total cost per additional unit between the two output levels.
variables.domain: Finite signed secant slope; not necessarily the derivative at either output level.
